toc.title: When you already have a growth mindset
When you have a fixed mindset
Your thoughts come from your state

blocks.p: Mindset is important, but I don't think it's your problem. I don't think the way you think is what's causing the problems you're seeking help for. Actually, if you focus on your thinking or on your mindset, you may end up very frustrated, or ready to give up on making change in your life altogether.
Let's go through why mindset is not your main problem, and what you can do instead to start making lasting change.
We'll start off really generally. Merriam-Webster says mindset is "a mental attitude or inclination." Cambridge Dictionary says it's "a person's way of thinking and their opinions."

If you search for mindset, you'll very quickly find Carol Dweck. I don't know if she's the one who started the whole mindset craze, but when you look up mindset, she comes up. What I'm more interested in is what Carol Dweck brought to the world of psychology, where it's gone from there, and why it's very incomplete.

She's the one who came up with the idea of growth mindset and fixed mindset. You've probably heard of this, but here's a quick summary from Verywell Mind. On fixed mindsets: "If you have a fixed mindset, you believe your abilities are fixed traits and therefore can't be changed. You may also believe that your talent and intelligence alone lead to success, and effort is not required." So the idea is that you believe that's it. You can't do better. You're born the way you're born.

On growth mindsets: "On the flip side, if you have a growth mindset, you believe that your talents and abilities can be developed over time through efforts and persistence. People with this mindset don't necessarily believe that everyone can become Einstein or Mozart just because they try. They do, however, believe that everyone can get smarter or more talented if they work at it." So with a growth mindset, you believe you can improve through effort, practice, failure, repetition, and further refinement.

From this view, your mindset is the problem. The way you think is the problem. That's not revolutionary in psychology. Many people in psychology have looked at thinking as the problem, the thing that needs to change. What Dweck and the people who adopt this way of thinking argue is that mindset can be the catalyst for change. If you change your mindset, specifically to a growth mindset, then the change you want will unfold based on effort. If you have a fixed mindset, that's the problem, and that's what needs to be addressed.

Is something wrong with your business? Are you not getting the right grades in school? Can you not communicate with your spouse effectively? Do you want a life partner and can't find one? Is there some emotional dysregulation you can't get over? All of these things, and a lot more, can supposedly be fixed with a growth mindset. Look these things up online and you'll easily find articles, books, courses, and videos applying the growth mindset idea to them.

It's huge. Many people believe in this growth mindset stuff. I have no idea if Carol Dweck intended it to be applied to all these areas, but that's where we're at. From this psychological point of view, the problem is that you have a fixed mindset, and the way to change it is through a growth mindset.
So identify something you want to change in your life. Something serious, something you really want to change. Got it? Now you know the answer is to adopt a growth mindset to fix your problem.
So go ahead and adopt that growth mindset. Did you get it? Do you have that growth mindset yet?

Some of you haven't gotten there yet. I don't think it worked for everybody. To have a growth mindset, you have to grow it. You can't just turn it on or off. So even though the problem is easily diagnosable, it's not easily fixed by simply adopting a growth mindset. You can't just choose to have one.
Psychology Today gives a list of fifteen ideas for how to adopt a growth mindset. Here are a handful:

ul: Replace negative thoughts with positive ones.

blocks.p: So again, go ahead and do that. Embrace imperfection now. Be your authentic self now. Replace your negative thoughts with positive ones. I'll wait right here.

Again, some of you didn't do it. It's more complex than just saying, think differently. If your mindset is the problem, the solution seems to be to just change your mindset. And these smaller pieces, like cultivating purpose, embracing imperfection, or replacing your negative thoughts with positive ones, are kind of like saying, "Well, just stop thinking that way. Think this way, so you can eventually have a growth mindset." It's all about thinking. Do this, think this way, don't think that way. That seems very inadequate to me. It doesn't seem like a healthy approach to tell someone to just stop doing that.

Why do some people have a growth mindset and some people have a fixed mindset? A couple of easy answers would be that it's based on how they were raised, or that whatever mindset they have, it's just easier to stick with those beliefs than to challenge them. Challenging them would be uncomfortable, and taking on a different way of thinking is hard, because emotionally you'd have to change along with it.

But either way, we're still basically saying that the individual doesn't think right. No matter the reason, we're saying you're not thinking right, and thinking is your problem. I don't find this line of thinking super helpful. Getting people to think differently is not easy, especially if that's your primary way of addressing someone's presenting problems. It's typically not just a thinking problem. It has to be more than that.

I've been a therapist for over fifteen years, and therapy clients don't change this way. They don't simply start thinking differently. I don't change this way either. My clients want change. They're motivated for change. They want to think differently. They don't want to blame and shame themselves and use their thoughts to inflict further discomfort on themselves. They want to think more positively, but for some reason they don't, at least not initially. Eventually, through therapy and the changes they make at home, they can begin to think more positively and get that growth mindset. But other things need to come into play first. It's not just about thinking differently.

blocks.h: When you already have a growth mindset

blocks.p: Let me come at this from a different angle. When is your mindset already more growth oriented? There are probably times when it already is, without you needing to choose it or cultivate it.

When do you have positive thoughts? When are you okay with learning from failure or obstacles? When do you feel more authentic? When do you need less approval from others? When are you okay with being imperfect? You probably already have moments like that. And if you never feel that way, imagine what it would look like to be more likely to feel that way.

I would guess your mindset changes when you're feeling calm and relaxed. You're more open to what life brings you: the flow of daily life, the emotions that come and go. You're more connected to the present moment and to your senses. When you're calm and relaxed, your failures and obstacles probably aren't debilitating. You're more likely to roll with them and learn from them.

I would guess you have a growth mindset when you're feeling motivated and focused, energized to keep moving forward, maybe toward a specific goal. You probably have more of a growth mindset when you're with people you feel safety and trust with, people you can be vulnerable with, or people you can have fun with. You probably have more of a growth mindset when you're playing a game and socializing.

Say you're playing cornhole, which I'm sure we all do. If you miss a throw, as long as you're with people and having a good time, it won't be debilitating. You'll pick up the sandbag and throw again. If you miss that one, which you probably will, you'll try again after that. You may not realize it, but in a sense, you have a growth mindset. You're seeing these little failures, like missing the hole, and trying to do better the next time.
So there are probably contexts in your life where you already have something like a growth mindset. Why would it be there in some contexts but not others?

blocks.h: When you have a fixed mindset

blocks.p: Now the other side. When do you have a fixed mindset? When do you have limiting beliefs? When are you more frustrated and think you'll fail? When do you feel there's no point in trying? When do you feel most like a loser, like you don't believe in yourself?

I would guess it's when you're more emotionally upset, when you're not calm or connected to the present moment. I would guess it's when you're feeling more alone or rejected, and when you're feeling pressured.

So your emotional state has a lot to do with how fixed or growth oriented your mindset is. It's not that you have this one or that one. Where you land on that spectrum depends on the context. The context of the situation matters, and so do your internal feelings, not just your mindset.

blocks.h: Your thoughts come from your state

blocks.p: Why would context and emotions influence your mindset? Because your thoughts don't exist on their own. You don't just have words in your brain that come and go. Well, you do, but they come and go based on the state of your body. And the state of your body depends on the context you're in, like how much safety or danger you're literally in, in your environment.

The Polyvagal Theory teaches us that the body can be in one of three basic states. It's more complex than this, but basically, the body can be prepared for safety and social engagement, for flight and fight, or for shutdown, a collapsed immobilization.

We evolved to survive, or to thrive, based on the context we're in. Even though we're not out in the wild being chased down by predators, these evolutionary instincts and behaviors are still alive within us. They're encoded into our DNA. This isn't something we choose. It's a state our body is in based on the needs of the situation, speaking generally.

ul: Flight and fight: when we're in danger, our sympathetic state activates, and we use aggression or flee the situation to survive.
Shutdown: when we're in a life threatening situation, we collapse and immobilize, and kind of play dead.
Safety: when we're safe, we can connect with each other, feel happiness, and mindfully attune to our senses and really experience being connected to the present moment.

blocks.p: Those are the basic states. There are also mixed states, including freeze, play, stillness, appeasement, intimacy, and arguably fawn, although I have my questions about that.

Depending on the state of your body, your emotions change too. In flight and fight, you feel things like anxiety, anger, irritation, and worry. In shutdown, you feel depression and numbness, alone and rejected. In safety, you feel calmer and relaxed, connected, fun, awe, happiness. Even if you're not literally running away, fighting, or collapsing, that biology can be active, and you'll feel it as these emotions.

Your body state dictates your emotional experience, but it also dictates other things: your sensations, your impulses, your behaviors, and your cognitions. By cognitions I mean word-based thoughts, beliefs, images, memories, ideas, calculations, pretty much anything your brain can do.
So mindset comes from the state of your body. Growth or fixed, it comes from your state.

ul: In your safety state, your thoughts are flavored with more hope, more compassion, and more focus. You're better able to learn and to think critically. Does that sound like a growth mindset or a fixed mindset?
In your flight and fight state, your thoughts are flavored with more avoidance and evasion, blaming others, and blaming yourself. More fixed, or more growth?
In your shutdown state, your mindset is flavored with more hopelessness and pointlessness. Fixed, or growth?

blocks.p: Irene Lyon said it this way on the podcast:

q: To be cognitive and use your mind, you have to have the other parts of your nervous system in a regulated state so the mind can function at its highest level possible.

blocks.p: Your mindset comes from your state, and your state comes from a few places.
It comes from the external world: the sensory cues in your environment, like lighting and sound, and also the people around you and the cues they're giving you.
It comes from the internal world. If you're hungry, that affects your state. You might get hangry, flavored with more fight activation. A chronic illness affects your state as well.

And it comes from your past. If you lived with good enough attachment with your caregivers, and good enough healthy boundaries, you're more likely to have a growth mindset, in my opinion. You'll be better able to roll with life's obstacles, think positively, have compassion for yourself and others, learn, and keep growing. If you were taught and modeled the importance of effort, you probably have a better chance of having a growth mindset.

Trauma, though, can severely limit someone's states. When I say trauma, I don't really mean the thing someone went through. Trauma is the impact on the body of the things they went through, or didn't go through, like good enough parenting. Those things can leave you in a state of flight or fight, shutdown, freeze, maybe appease, and arguably fawn. Trauma is being stuck in a defensive state. It means you can't access your safety state, or have great difficulty accessing it and keeping access to it.
Mindset is important, of course. But I would argue it's not as important as your state. Your state is the primary mover. If your state changes, your mindset changes along with it.

If you try to change your mindset while you're in a defensive state, say you're angry and in fight, and I tell you to think differently, it's probably not going to go very well. You can try, but you'll likely end up pretty frustrated, and it might just reinforce the fixed mindset. You'll probably end up blaming yourself or somebody else, or saying how stupid this mindset stuff is: "I knew it. I never should have tried in the first place."

Those who have a growth mindset probably have enough access to their safety state. When obstacles come up, or they have a failure or a mini failure, they don't sink into defensive activation. They don't get stuck in flight, fight, or shutdown. They can feel anxiety, maybe even anger, but it doesn't weigh them down and stop them from moving forward. They can feel it, experience it, and maybe even use it as motivation to learn and do better next time.

That person has a pretty darn good anchor in their safety state. That's probably the biggest difference between someone with a growth mindset and someone with a fixed mindset. They didn't change their thinking overnight. They didn't just decide to have a growth mindset. Their underlying bodily state allows for it. Without access to their safety state, they'd probably have just as fixed a mindset as anybody else stuck in a defensive state.
So when people with enough safety activation see someone who doesn't think like them, probably someone in more of a defensive state, they identify the problem as how that person thinks.
Thinking is a problem, but it's not the problem. Here's how I think of it:

ol: The secondary problem is the sensations and impulses that come from that state and haven't been felt and acted on.
The tertiary problem, the one you probably notice, is the emotions and cognitions that come from that state.

blocks.p: So state is the primary problem. How do you change it? It's not easy, but it is possible to change the underlying state and get into more of your safety state.

ol: Have actual safety around you. You need literal, actual, factual environmental safety, a safe enough environment. If you're in a dangerous environment, it's going to be very difficult to have a growth mindset. You also need actual safe people in your life. With people who are causing you harm or are a direct danger to you, it's going to be very, very difficult to have a growth mindset.

Practice feeling safe. Assuming you have a safe enough environment and people, you practice feeling safe through mindfulness, through connecting to the present moment, and through your senses. Notice which sense is most accessible for you. If you have a really good sense of smell or taste, use that. Use it really slowly, and experience what it's like to use that sense and what it tells you. That can help you access more connection to the present moment and to yourself, which helps you access your safety state. Other ways to practice feeling safe are movement, music, and being with safe others: anything that helps you feel more connected to the present moment, to yourself, or to others. If you feel connection, that's a really good sign you're in your safety state. Practice it more and more.

Feel your defensive activation. Eventually, once you've built the strength of your safety state, you'll be able to feel your defensive activation with compassion and curiosity: your sadness, your feelings of being alone or rejected, your anger and anxiety. As you feel those while you're grounded and connected to the present moment, to yourself, or to others, they can soften. That changes your state as well.

blocks.p: None of this is easy. Saying "fix your mindset" is easy. The actual work of changing your state is not. But it is possible, especially over time. The priority is building the strength of your safety state. If you can do that, you can heal your traumatized state, or relieve your stuck defensive state. And as that happens, you have more access to your safety state, which keeps the process unfolding.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.
